The useful part of this note isn’t JPMorgan’s rating. It’s the rare, specific look at what Tesla is telling investors behind closed doors at Fremont right now. Read it that way, and every line is a Tesla claim, filtered through an analyst who just sell stocks.

Stack the four claims against Tesla’s own record and the pattern is hard to miss. FSD v15 is a “step-change,” just like v14 and v13. HW4 does unsupervised driving, just like HW3 was supposed to. The Cybercab is about to scale, into a service, Robotaxi, that has been stuck in neutral for a year. Optimus goes on sale in 2027, despite Tesla showing nothing about the program in half a year.

We’ll believe unsupervised FSD on HW4 when a customer car does it, and Tesla takes responsibility, which might never happen. [...] ## HW4 can handle it — the same thing Tesla said about HW3

Tesla told the bank that its current HW4 computer, which it calls AI4, is enough to run v15 and unsupervised FSD. At the same time, Tesla is rolling out AI4.5, a new version of the chip with roughly 10% more compute and about twice the memory.

Tesla made that exact promise about the previous computer, HW3, for years before quietly walking it back. # Tesla says FSD v15 is a ‘step-change,’ Optimus sells in 2027

Avatar for Fred Lambert  Fred Lambert | Aug 20 2026 - 12:37 pm PT

155 Comments

Tesla (TSLA) montreal 

Tesla laid out an updated timeline for Full Self-Driving, its Cybercab, and the Optimus robot in a recent meeting with JPMorgan at its Fremont factory. The bank walked away with claims that FSD v15 is a “step-change,” that today’s HW4 computer can handle unsupervised driving, and that Optimus could go on sale to outside buyers as soon as the second half of 2027.

Most of it repeats promises Tesla has made, and missed, before.

## FSD v15: a “step-change,” according to Tesla

results.content:
The core difference is liability and scope. A supervised system can roll out to a large fleet fast, because the driver absorbs responsibility. A driverless fleet must prove safety for each service area before it charges a fare. Tesla trades autonomy for reach. Waymo and Zoox trade reach for autonomy. V15 does not change that structure, even if the network improves.

Hardware cost follows from the same split. A fleet operator can spread an expensive sensor and compute package across many paid miles. Tesla must make its package cheap enough to put in every car it sells. That is why the in-car computer is not a side detail. It sets the ceiling on what the network can do for a customer who paid for a regular car.

## Historical Context and Regulatory Limits [...] | Hardware | What Tesla has said | What reports say | V15 status |
------|
| AI4 computer | Cars stay on AI4 for now, per Musk | Expected to receive v15 and new visuals | Likely, not confirmed |
| AI5 computer | Aimed first at the Optimus robot, per Musk | Not planned for new passenger cars initially | Not a v15 factor yet |
| AI3 / Hardware 3 | No statement found | One report says it may be excluded | Unconfirmed |
| All configurations | No complete list published | Varies by outlet | Open |

## AI5 and Optimus: Why New Silicon Is Not Reaching Cars First [...] Musk has said AI5 is intended first for Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot, and that passenger cars stay on AI4 for now. That ordering is a notable inversion of Tesla’s old story. For years the company pitched each new car computer as the key to self-driving. Now the newest chip goes to a robot first.

There is a plausible engineering reason, though it is our reading and not a Tesla statement. A robot sells in small volumes and can absorb an expensive computer. A car that ships by the hundreds of thousands cannot. Tesla also has millions of cars on the road with older chips, so a network that demands the newest silicon would strand a large part of the fleet. Our earlier analysis of Musk’s AI4, AI5 and AI6 cadence claims reached a similar conclusion about the economics.

results.title: Tesla plans big safety improvements for Full Self-Driving v15
results.content:
A tighter comparison uses the same Tesla fleet. Cars driven manually with active safety features such as automatic emergency braking still recorded a major collision about every 2.1 million miles. Against that baseline, FSD’s advantage shrinks to roughly 2.4 to 2.7 times fewer severe crashes, which independent researchers argue is the more apples-to-apples figure.

European data released in 2026 pointed in the same direction: Tesla reported FSD as 3.5 times safer than manual driving in the Netherlands and 4.1 times fewer collisions than manually driven Teslas with active safety across more than 100 million kilometers in five approved countries. [...] - Upgraded vision encoder shared between FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus, which is trained on millions of internet videos for improved generalization and data efficiency, improving the critical intervention rate by 25x.
- Introduced Tesla Augmented Reality, replacing all of the explicit model signals into a single end-to-end visualization using less total compute.
- Improved navigation by using an end-to-end learned model based on route preference data from the fleet.
- Improved parking location selection by using personalized parking history, and the map will now display multiple parking options at your destination.
- Improved driver monitoring by increasing vision-based attention monitoring availability with hats and sunglasses and decreasing strictness in higher speed driver profiles. [...] Those numbers do not settle every debate. NHTSA’s Standing General Order still shows Tesla accounting for the large majority of U.S. Level 2 driver-assist crash reports, in part because the fleet logs far more assisted miles than rivals. Critics also note that Tesla’s “U.S. average” mixes crash definitions and driving mix.

Even so, Tesla’s own same-car comparisons, plus lower rates of automatic emergency braking and harsh maneuvers when FSD is engaged, are the evidence Elluswamy is pointing to when he says v15 will push prediction and collision avoidance further. The claim is not that software already eliminates risk. It is that each major version is meant to widen the gap between the system and an unaided human driver.
